A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, dataset construction and specificity framework. Their main text, figures, tables and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original human preference and specificity-judgment studies, COCO-based ranking analyses, and VLM length-constraint experiments in Section 4 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds hallucination tests, contrast-set sensitivity experiments and statistical analyses of potential confounds.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same caption-construction conditions and specificity measure based on the target image's CLIPScore rank. The new perturbation and subsampling procedures evaluate this existing measure.

E1.justification: Section 4.2.1 adds a corrupted-caption test scenario using targeted hallucinations in 37 composite captions. The underlying COCO coverage and human tasks remain unchanged; LAION-5B is suggested as a possible contrast-image source but is not evaluated.

E2.justification: The original, verbose, composite and image-to-text comparison conditions, along with the three length-constraint conditions, are retained. Newly cited hallucination metrics are not evaluated as additional comparators.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs introduce three hallucinated variants per verified caption, ten contrast-set sizes from 3 to 4,999, and word-frequency/readability controls in preference analyses. Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendix A also revise the reported generator from GPT-4o to GPT-4o-mini, aligning with v1's Section 3.1; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Sections 4.2.1–4.2.2 test whether hallucinations inflate specificity and whether findings depend on contrast-set size. Additional word-frequency/readability controls and an image-random-intercept analysis investigate confounds beyond v1's validation. The earlier length-prompt case study and Appendix D studies are retained.

E5.justification: The new sensitivity analysis specifies 100 repeated subsamples per caption. v2 also adds t-test and mixed-effects inference, while retaining the earlier bootstrap confidence intervals and human-study regression reporting. These additions do not indicate increased repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports ranks across ten contrast-set sizes, preserving the Image-to-Text, Composite, Original, Verbose ordering. Hallucination perturbations increase mean rank from 17.05 to 30.91 (p=0.017). Section 4.2 replaces v1's comparable-ranks description with an explicitly significant original–verbose difference (beta=-7.35, p<0.001). Earlier primary and Appendix D numerical results are retained.

T1.justification: The possible-worlds and entailment motivation, contrast-relative specificity definition and rank construction remain unchanged. v2 adds no formal theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims that length is an unreliable specificity proxy, human preferences track specificity, and length-constraint strategies matter. The added validation supports these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds possible CLIP training-data overlap as an explanation for the original–verbose gap, interprets the new robustness analyses, and expands discussion of encoder bias and hallucinations. It also clarifies that verbosity is experimentally manipulated and that specificity does not measure user relevance, substantially extending the applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 documents the hallucination-generation prompt and new analysis specifications, and corrects several GPT-4o references to GPT-4o-mini. Figure 5 nevertheless retains GPT-4o labels. Existing caption prompts, hardware/runtime disclosures and code/data access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges Young et al. (2014) as a denotation-graph precedent and adds Graesser et al. (2014), Oh and Hwang (2026), Petryk et al. (2024), and Schuhmann et al. (2022). These support focused additions on readability, hallucinations and contrast-image sourcing without substantially restructuring the research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 adds two results subsections, expands the limitations discussion and makes localized wording, terminology and acknowledgment edits. The main section sequence and Appendices A–D remain intact, and most retained prose closely matches v1.

P2.justification: v2 adds the contrast-set results as Table 2; the existing appendix example table becomes Table 3. Figures 1–7 and the example-table content are retained, with some relocation and page reflow. Appendix D's participant instructions are reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the existing conclusions through confound controls and targeted robustness checks, and gives a more qualified interpretation of the original–verbose gap. These are useful but bounded gains: the hallucination test covers 37 captions, and the image-random-intercept analysis does not establish v2's stronger assertion that encoder biases are constant across description types. Overall, the evidence and qualifications improve despite remaining methodological uncertainty.
